title: Surface phenomena and adsorption. Chromatography. Qualitative reactions based on adsorption. Quantitative assessment of adsorption

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of surface energy and surface tension, surface-active and surface-inactive substances, adsorption, desorption, absorption and chemisorption, the laws of adsorption on mobile and immobile surfaces (the Gibbs, Langmuir and Freundlich equations), and chromatographic methods and their significance in medicine.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of surface energy, surface tension and surface activity;
surface-active, surface-inactive and surface-indifferent substances, and the Duclaux–Traube rule;
the difference between adsorption, absorption, desorption and chemisorption;
the Gibbs, Langmuir and Freundlich equations;
ion-exchange adsorption and the Paneth–Fajans rule;
the principles and types of chromatography and the R~f~ value.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the amount adsorbed from experimental data;
analyze an adsorption isotherm;
calculate R~f~ on a paper or thin-layer chromatogram;
justify the medical use of sorbents and surfactants.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Adsorption** is the accumulation of a substance on the **surface** of another phase; **absorption** is its uptake throughout the **volume**. Surface-active substances lower surface tension and are adsorbed positively at the surface (Γ > 0).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: A surfactant molecule — **“head in the water, tail in the air”**: the polar hydrophilic “head” (−COO^−^, −OH, −SO~3~^−^) sits in the water, the nonpolar hydrophobic hydrocarbon “tail” in the air or oil.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Activated charcoal also adsorbs drugs: drugs taken at the same time (contraceptives, antibiotics) become less effective. That is why other drugs are taken at least 1.5–2 hours before or after charcoal.

blocks.text: A molecule inside a phase is attracted equally from all sides, whereas a molecule at the surface is acted on by a resultant force directed inward. That is why the surface layer has excess energy — **surface energy**. The free surface energy per unit area is called **surface tension** (σ), J/m^2^ or N/m.

A system spontaneously tends to reduce its surface energy: drops take a spherical shape (the smallest surface), small drops merge into larger ones, and substances that lower σ accumulate at the surface. Water has a very high surface tension: ≈ 73 mN/m at 20 °C.

parts.text: **Hay’s test:** sulfur powder is sprinkled on the surface of urine. Normally the powder stays on the surface; if the urine contains bile acids (strong surfactants), surface tension falls and the powder sinks — the test is positive in obstructive jaundice and liver diseases.

items: **Surface-active substances (surfactants)** lower the surface tension of the solvent and accumulate at the surface: alcohols, carboxylic acids, soaps, bile acids, phospholipids, proteins. They have a **diphilic** (amphiphilic) structure.
**Surface-inactive substances** slightly raise the surface tension and move away from the surface into the bulk (negative adsorption): strong electrolytes (NaCl, KNO~3~), inorganic acids and alkalis.
**Surface-indifferent substances** hardly change the surface tension: glucose, sucrose.

blocks.text: **Surface activity** is the ability of a substance to lower surface tension: g = −dσ / dC. **The Duclaux–Traube rule:** in a homologous series, each CH~2~ group added to the hydrocarbon radical increases the surface activity **3–3.5 times** (formic < acetic < propionic < butyric acid).

parts.text: **Pulmonary surfactant** is a mixture of phospholipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and proteins that lines the inner surface of the alveoli. By Laplace’s law the collapsing pressure of an alveolus is P = 2σ / r; surfactant sharply lowers σ and prevents the alveoli from collapsing on expiration. When surfactant is lacking in preterm infants, **respiratory distress syndrome** develops; it is treated by giving natural or synthetic surfactant into the trachea.

blocks.text: **Sorption** is the uptake of one substance by another. The substance that takes up is the **sorbent** (adsorbent), and the substance taken up is the **sorbate** (adsorptive).

blocks.text: Adsorption is an **exothermic** process: as temperature rises, adsorption decreases and desorption increases. How much is adsorbed depends on the **specific surface area** of the sorbent: the inner pore surface of 1 g of activated charcoal reaches 500–1500 m^2^.

sections.title: 4. Adsorption on a mobile surface. The Gibbs equation

blocks.text: Liquid–gas and liquid–liquid boundaries are **mobile surfaces**. Adsorption of a solute at such a surface is described by the **Gibbs equation**: Γ = −(C / R·T)·(dσ / dC), where Γ is the surface excess (mol/m^2^).

items: If dσ / dC < 0 (surfactant), Γ > 0 — **positive adsorption**, the substance accumulates at the surface.
If dσ / dC > 0 (surface-inactive substance), Γ < 0 — **negative adsorption**, the substance moves from the surface into the bulk.

Surfactant molecules are **oriented** at the surface: as the concentration grows they stand upright and form a dense monomolecular layer (a “palisade”) — this is the physicochemical basis of the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane.

sections.title: 5. Adsorption on a solid surface. The Langmuir and Freundlich equations

blocks.text: **Langmuir’s theory of monomolecular adsorption:** adsorption occurs at the active sites of the sorbent; each site holds one molecule; when the surface is filled, a monomolecular layer is formed. **Langmuir equation:** Γ = Γ~∞~·K·C / (1 + K·C), where Γ~∞~ is the maximum (full-layer) adsorption and K is the adsorption constant.

items: At low concentration (K·C ≪ 1): Γ ≈ Γ~∞~·K·C — adsorption is proportional to concentration.
At high concentration (K·C ≫ 1): Γ ≈ Γ~∞~ — the surface is saturated.
**The empirical Freundlich equation** (for medium concentrations): x / m = K·C^1/n^; in logarithmic form lg(x / m) = lgK + (1 / n)·lgC — a straight line from which K and 1/n are found.

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Adsorption isotherm (by the Langmuir equation): a linear region at low concentration and saturation approaching Γ~∞~ at high concentration (left); the logarithmic form of the Freundlich equation (right) (drawn from calculated data).

blocks.text: **Quantitative assessment of adsorption:** after the sorbent is placed in a solution and equilibrium is reached, adsorption is found from the decrease in the concentration of the solution: Γ = (C~0~ − C)·V / m, where C~0~ and C are the initial and equilibrium concentrations, V the volume of solution and m the mass of sorbent.

sections.title: 6. Adsorption of electrolytes and ion exchange

blocks.text: **The Paneth–Fajans rule:** the surface of a crystal selectively adsorbs ions that are part of its lattice or isomorphous with them. For example, AgI crystals adsorb I^−^ in a solution with excess KI, and Ag^+^ with excess AgNO~3~ — this is how the charge of a colloidal particle arises (topic 8).

**Ion-exchange adsorption:** the sorbent gives one of its own ions to the solution and takes up an equivalent amount of another ion in its place. Such sorbents are called **ion exchangers**: **cation exchangers** (R−SO~3~H, exchange cations) and **anion exchangers** (R−N(CH~3~)~3~^+^OH^−^, exchange anions).

blocks.text: **Chromatography** is a method of separation and analysis based on the different distribution (selective adsorption) of the components of a mixture between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. It was discovered in 1903 by the Russian botanist **M.S. Tsvet**, who separated plant pigments in a column packed with chalk.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Classification of chromatographic methods
head: Criterion
Types
rows: adsorption, partition, ion-exchange, gel filtration (by molecular size), affinity (by specific binding)
column, paper, thin-layer (TLC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)

blocks.text: In paper and thin-layer chromatography the movement of a substance is described by the **R~f~ value**: R~f~ = l / L, where l is the distance from the start line to the spot of the substance and L is the distance from the start line to the solvent front. Under given conditions R~f~ is constant for each substance — the substance is identified by it.

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Chromatogram of leaf pigments: carotenoids (yellow), chlorophyll a (blue-green) and chlorophyll b (yellowish green) have risen with the solvent to different distances and formed separate spots — a modern version of M.S. Tsvet’s experiment (Wikimedia Commons).

parts.text: In medicine: **HPLC** — glycated hemoglobin (HbA~1c~), vitamins, drug concentrations in the blood; **gas chromatography** — ethanol in blood and urine, toxicological examination; **paper and TLC** — amino acids, screening for inherited aminoacidopathies (phenylketonuria); **gel filtration and affinity chromatography** — purification of proteins, antibodies and vaccines.

items: Determine the initial concentration of the solution (C~0~) (by titration or photometry).
Put an accurately weighed portion of sorbent (m) into a known volume of solution (V) and shake until equilibrium is reached.
Filter and determine the equilibrium concentration (C).
Calculate the adsorption with the formula Γ = (C~0~ − C)·V / m (mmol/g).
Repeat at several concentrations and plot the isotherm Γ = f(C).

skills.title: Skill: determining R~f~ on a chromatogram

items: Draw a start line with a graphite pencil 1.5–2 cm above the bottom of the paper or plate.
Apply the sample and the standards as small spots with a capillary and dry them.
Place the plate in a chamber with solvent so that the start line is above the solvent.
When the solvent front reaches the top, remove the plate, mark the front and dry it; stain colorless substances with a developing reagent (ninhydrin for amino acids).
Measure l and L, calculate R~f~ = l / L and compare with the standards.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: In a study of the adsorption of methylene blue, 0.5 g of activated charcoal was added to 50 mL of a 0.002 M solution. After equilibrium the concentration fell to 0.0004 M.
cases.ask: Calculate the adsorption capacity of the charcoal (mmol/g). What does this experiment show for medicine?
cases.answer: Γ = (C~0~ − C)·V / m = (0.002 − 0.0004) · 0.05 / 0.5 = 0.0016 · 0.1 = 0.00016 mol/g = 0.16 mmol/g. 80 % of the dye passed onto the charcoal. Because of this property, activated charcoal binds toxins, alkaloids and drugs in the gastrointestinal tract — it is effective in acute oral poisoning if given early (within 1 hour).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: An infant born at week 29 of pregnancy develops shortness of breath, nasal flaring and chest retractions a few hours after birth. The X-ray shows a “ground-glass” appearance of the lungs.
cases.ask: What is the condition? What is its physicochemical basis and the principle of treatment?
cases.answer: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease). Pulmonary surfactant is produced in sufficient amounts only by about weeks 34–36 of pregnancy; in a preterm infant it is lacking, and surface tension in the alveoli remains high. By Laplace’s law (P = 2σ / r) small alveoli collapse on expiration (atelectasis). Treatment: surfactant preparation given into the trachea, respiratory support (CPAP); when there is a risk, glucocorticoids are given to the mother before delivery (they speed up surfactant synthesis).

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A blood sample from a newborn was examined by paper chromatography. The solvent front rose 12.0 cm above the start line, and a strong spot in the sample was located at 6.6 cm. Under these conditions the R~f~ of standard phenylalanine is 0.55.
cases.ask: Calculate the R~f~ of the spot. What may the result indicate?
cases.answer: R~f~ = 6.6 / 12.0 = 0.55 — it matches standard phenylalanine. A strong phenylalanine spot in the blood indicates that it is increased, that is, possible **phenylketonuria**. The diagnosis is confirmed by a quantitative method (tandem mass spectrometry or fluorimetry); treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet.
